Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

vignette: John, a 77-year-old African-American man and retired software engineer, has been struggling with the haunting memories of his traumatic past as a refugee. John immigrated to America years ago after enduring unspeakable horrors in a war-torn country where he witnessed violence and was forced into dire living conditions. His symptoms have escalated recently, particularly when triggered by authority commands or other trauma-related events. When he hears someone issue orders or instructions, his mind immediately goes back to the oppressive military presence that haunted him during those dark days. This triggering is not just a fleeting thought; it often leads to feelings of disassociation and detachment, making John feel as though he's observing himself from afar. John has come to believe that going out into public spaces only exacerbates these triggers, so he increasingly avoids leaving his home. His wife has noticed this behavior and worries about the isolation he imposes on himself. Even within the familiar confines of their home, a sudden noise or command can jolt him back to those terrifying moments, making it impossible for John to fully relax. John's memories of the traumatic events are fragmented but vividly visual. He recalls specific snapshots of that time as distinct images in his mind, often emotionless and detached. This detachment serves as both a coping mechanism and a source of distress. When he tries to recall those moments, they feel like scenes from someone else's life. These dissociated memories are further compounded by the maladaptive strategies John employs. To cope with these intrusive thoughts and feelings, John has developed several avoidance behaviors that have taken root over time. He avoids not only going out but also interacting with other people, believing this will keep him safe from potential triggers. However, this isolation is a double-edged sword; it provides temporary relief but exacerbates his fear of re-experiencing the trauma. John's mind constantly seeks to distract itself by keeping occupied at all times. His thoughts are always racing, often focused on mundane tasks and activities that serve as an escape from the intrusive memories. This mental distraction has become a key part of how he navigates daily life, but it also means he rarely allows himself time for introspection or genuine relaxation. The interplay between his triggers, memory, and maladaptive strategies creates a vicious cycle that tightens over time. When John encounters something that reminds him of the traumatic events-whether an authority figure giving orders or a sudden noise-he immediately feels detached and numb. These feelings reinforce his belief that he needs to avoid such situations entirely, leading to further isolation and avoidance behaviors. This avoidance, in turn, exacerbates the intensity of his memories. The less John engages with the world around him, the more vivid and intrusive these fragmented images become. He is certain that if he were to face these triggers head-on, they would overwhelm him completely. As a result, he remains trapped within this cycle, believing it's the only way to maintain any semblance of normalcy. John's relationship with his wife has been strained by these behaviors. She notices how her husband withdraws from family activities and becomes increasingly isolated. John is aware that this pattern is affecting his life but feels helpless to break free from it. He had come to believe that constant mental distraction and avoidance were the only ways to keep himself safe. What finally brought John to seek help was a growing sense of loneliness and the realization that he could no longer bear the weight of these memories alone. Despite his fears, he is hopeful that with professional guidance, he might find a way to confront these triggers without being overwhelmed by them. The thought of reclaiming some normalcy in his daily life motivates him as he embarks on this journey toward healing.
